newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan reiterates need for risky loan checks.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan reiterates need for risky loan checks.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Monday that U.S. regulators increasingly scrutinize bank management practices instead of checking scores of loans to find risks to the financial system.

Speaking to the Federation of Bankers Associations in Tokyo, the central bank chief said the growing volume and complexity of transactions at the biggest banks was forcing regulators to change their methods.
"While still important, the amount of transaction testing, especially at large banks, will decline," Greenspan said.
A text of his remarks was issued in Washington.

The U.S. central bank chief told Japanese authorities, who are preparing for a five-year "Big Bang" to liberalize Japan's financial markets, that authorities need to try to ensure that banks have the means and expertise to control risk.
"The better these risk information and control systems, the more risk a bank can prudently assume," Greenspan said.
But he suggested central banks and governments should not try to totally insulate private institutions from all losses because doing so can lead to laxity.
"Such laxity would hold the potential of a major call on taxpayers," Greenspan said.
He said central banks must prevent big financial market disruptions, but not stop private institutions from taking prudent risks even if doing so results in losses or failures.
"Our goal as supervisors...should not be to prevent all bank failures, but to maintain suffient prudential standards so that banking problems which do occur do not become widespread," he said.

Japan is aiming to open its markets by 2001, ending fixed commissions for stockbrokers, increasing the flow of financial information and allowing banks, insurance companies and securities firms to compete more freely.
Greenspan said the Fed was initiating a review of internal credit risk and allocation models used by major U.S. banks to design, price and manage products like credit derivatives.

He said some bankers fear that new technologies will curb their profits by driving down spreads. But he added that technological change and competition were inevitable and said "banks unwilling or unable to adapt to them will lose market share and suffer lower risk adjusted rates of return."
Greenspan said the Group of Seven countries -- the United States, Japan, Britain, Canada, Germany, France and Italy -- want to coperate more in supervising financial institutions.
He said it was specially important to enhance supervision in emerging market economies for their sake and for the sake of global financial stability.
In addition, Greenspan said G7 leaders agree on the need to consider potential risks from so-called electronic money in which computers shift funds without money actually moving.

The Fed chief said he saw no threat to global stability from electronic money but said it was important for central banks to understand how the technology was developing and what it might mean for future dealing and regulation.
